pages.act: Guarantee of Temporary Residence and Labour
pages.text:
VALLEY SEASON

Kingdom of Marigni · Guarantee of Temporary Residence and Labour

No. VS-18-0947 · Issued by the Ministry of the Interior, Kingdom of Marigni · Countersigned by the Chancery of the Duchy of Valewisp

Pursuant to the provisions of Chapter Fourteen of the Basic Law of Marigni concerning the temporary residence of foreign nationals, and to the customary practice governing labour on the demesnes of the Duchy of Valewisp, the guarantor named below hereby provides full guarantee for the temporary residence and labour of the guaranteed party named below.

I. Guarantor
Lord of Maplegate Estate in the Duchy of Valewisp, Member of the House of Nobles
Baron Ludwig von Alder

II. Scope and Term of Permission
The guaranteed party is permitted to reside within the bounds of Maplegate Estate, north district of Valehold, Duchy of Valewisp, and to perform labour relating to the management of the estate. The term of permission is thirty days entire, counted from the date of arrival. Where no renewal is obtained upon expiry, the guaranteed party is required to depart the territory of the Kingdom of Marigni within seven days.

III. Responsibilities of the Guarantor
The nature of the guaranteed party’s labour is the supervision and management of estate operations, of domestic staff and of internal affairs; the address of residence is within the main manor house. The guarantor accepts joint liability for the conduct of the guaranteed party during the term of permission, and undertakes to provide lodging, board, and remuneration for labour to the value of 150 guldmark.

IV. Obligations of the Guaranteed Party
The guaranteed party shall observe the laws of the Kingdom of Marigni, the local ordinances of the Duchy of Valewisp, and the customs of the jurisdiction of residence. The guaranteed party shall not engage in activity exceeding the scope of permission, nor publicly propagate any religious, ideological or political doctrine contrary to the provisions of Chapter Seven of the Basic Law.

V. Protection of the Sacred Flame
For the duration of the permission, the guaranteed party enjoys rights of protection under the Sacred Flame equal to those of subjects of Marigni, and bears the obligations corresponding thereto.

VI. Signature and Seal
Both parties hereby confirm that every particular set out in this document is accurate. The guarantor confirms acceptance of the joint liability set out in Section III. The guaranteed party confirms understanding and acceptance of all obligations set out in Sections IV and V.

Signed, guarantor: von Alder    Date: 27 September 2018
Signed, guaranteed party: ______    Date: 25 September 2018

Ministry of the Interior, Kingdom of Marigni · Seal Forged in the Sacred Flame | Chancery of the Duchy of Valewisp · Seal of the Duchy

pages.heading: What the Agent Said
pages.text:
“The Duchy of Valewisp. Maplegate Estate.”

When the middleman pushes the document across the desk to your side, outside the window Forgehold is coming down with something between fog and fine rain, and the silver-grey light has stained every sheet of paper in his office the same colour.

“The lord is badly in want of a temporary steward. The last one left suddenly. There was no handover at all. Harvest is on them, and the estate has had nobody running it for close to three weeks.”

He is not looking at you. He is squaring up another stack of papers.

“Thirty-day term, board and lodging found, reasonable pay. The work over in Valewisp is not complicated, but somebody has to go at once.”

He closes the folder.

“Though I will say this. Baron von Alder being willing to guarantee a foreigner — that is not an opportunity you see often.”

pages.heading: The Baron’s Assessment
pages.text:
Baron von Alder saw you at the duchy’s chambers in Forgehold.

The meeting was short. His office faces north and gets no sun. On the wall hangs a small painting of Maplegate Estate, the one thing in the room that is not a document.

He went through your record. He asked two questions, both about accounts. He did not look up while you answered.

The second question was: if there is an item of expenditure in a ledger that you cannot make sense of, what do you do first.

“That will do,” he said. Then he signed the guarantee and pushed it back to the middleman. The whole thing took under fifteen minutes.

He was already reading something else as you stood up. At the door you looked back once at the painting.

When you came out of the chambers the Forgehold sky was still that silver grey. You had a railway ticket gripped in your hand.

pages.heading: The Kingdom’s Central Station
pages.text:
The station stands downstream on the River Forgel, at the edge of the south-bank quarter of Forgehold.

The hall is a domed building of the grey-green stone of the northern ranges, and the light pours down from narrow windows high in the dome and is cut by dust in the air into visible columns. Where steel meets stone the joins are made with extreme precision. The architecture of this city looks as though it grew out of the rock, and also as though it were cast, block by block, by somebody with enormous patience.

The air on the platform is cold, carrying the metal of the rails and the damp of the river further off. Several trains stand quietly at rest, dark grey bodies, copper window frames, no advertising and no unnecessary markings — only the service number and the name of the destination, set into the side of each carriage in small copper letters.

Your train is the 08:40. The terminus is Valehold North.

Looking back, the upper town on the north bank of the River Forgel shows only its outline in the morning fog: the spires of Crownblaze Palace, the dome of the Sanctum, and the stone span of the King’s Leap running together into one pale grey skyline. You never got over there to see it. Perhaps you never will.

You board, find your seat and stow your case. The carriage door closes very quietly.

pages.heading: Leaving the Mountains
pages.text:
The carriage goes dark as the train runs into the first tunnel.

Between Forgehold and Valehold the railway passes through three tunnels and two passes on the southern face of the northern ranges. These works fall directly under the Crown Lands, and every so often along the line you can see a small checkpoint and signal post beside the trackbed. Some of them look very old, with moss on the stone, and the signal lamps are new.

The air in a tunnel has a coolness particular to being underground. Not cold. A calm left behind after the rock has taken the temperature out of it.

Coming out of the longest one, the light floods in all at once.

pages.heading: The Country Changes
pages.text:
The south face of the range and the north face are two different worlds.

The north face, the Forgehold side, is grey. Bare rock, thin cover, a sky like something washed and not dried. On the south face the colours suddenly multiply: conifer gives way to mixed woodland, and among the dark green firs there begin to be gold birches and oaks in the middle of turning. The land falls away. The valley opens out.

The train works slowly down the valley of a tributary. Outside the window the canopy goes from grey-green to yellow-green to gold, as though somebody had laid the colour on in coats along both sides of the line. The air is different too: less of the cold of metal, and more of a smell both sweet and heavy, which you will learn later is leaf mould.

Now and then you pass a small town, with people on the platform waiting for other trains. They are dressed more easily than people in Forgehold, and in warmer colours.

Nobody notices you.

pages.heading: Valewisp
pages.text:
After the third halt the ground levels out altogether.

Outside the window is farmland and pasture at large, wheat spread along both banks of the river. Some of it is cut already, leaving even stubble and turned black earth; some of it is still waiting, the full heads bowing in the wind, a deep gold verging on amber. On the hills further off there are stretches of woodland, and autumn has dyed them into ragged copper-red banners.

Cattle move slowly along the field banks. One estate shows its roof from behind a stand of trees, and thin smoke from the cooking fire is coming off a chimney on the slate.

You do not know whose estate that is. You know only that the one you are going to is further north, up in the hills.

The train begins to slow.

pages.heading: Valehold North
pages.text:
The larger and more formal station is Valehold’s main one, in the centre of the town. Against it, the north station is a small stop with two tracks, the platform laid with the same grey-green slabs as in Forgehold, grass growing up through the joints. The waiting-room door stands half open on an empty room, and on the wall are a notice of the duchy’s forestry decrees and a timetable of this season’s markets.

You carry your luggage out off the platform. Late September afternoon; there is still some strength in the sun, but you can smell autumn in the wind.

On the open ground beside the platform stands a two-wheeled cart, the plain kind, dark wooden body, nothing about it for show. In the shafts is a grey-brown working horse of middling size, standing quietly and chewing.

A man is standing by the cart. Fifties, in a dark coat washed pale, the brim of his hat low. When he sees you he gives one nod and says nothing. He comes over and lifts your case onto the rack at the back of the cart. Not quickly, but exactly.

Then he goes back to the driver’s seat and waits for you to get up.

Through all of it there is not one word of greeting.

pages.heading: The Road In
pages.text:
The cart turns onto a dirt road kept in reasonable repair, with cut wheat fields and scattered fruit trees on either side.

The wheels make a regular grinding on the hard ground. Gregor — you learn his name later — sits in front driving, his back to you, his spine very straight. The hooves are the only rhythm on this stretch of road.

You try to take stock of it. From here you can see the line of the hills to the north with dark woodland along the top. To the south is open valley, and the River Valenne bends once in the distance, the surface of it giving back the afternoon light. The air is sweeter than at the station, and quieter, and you realise it has been a long time since you last heard quiet like it.

You pass a fork with a signpost giving the directions in two scripts. The upper line is in an old language you cannot read; the lower is in the common tongue. North: Maplegate Estate, four kilometres.

Gregor turns the horse.

pages.heading: The Avenue
pages.text:
At the end of the last rise, maples appear suddenly along both sides of the road.

The branches meet overhead, and the two even rows make a tunnel of it. Just now, in the last days of September, the tunnel is burning: gold leaves, copper leaves, deep orange not yet turned red, layer on layer, and the light coming through the gaps and falling on the flagstones like broken gold leaf. Every so often one leaf lets go and turns slowly in the air, and comes down on the horse’s mane.

The cart is under five minutes on Maplegate Avenue.

Ahead, the outline of a group of buildings shows between the crowns: stone walls, wooden-shingled roofs, one chimney smoking.

The estate.

Gregor pulls up, gets down and lifts your luggage off the rack. He sets it on the steps at the main door of the estate, and then speaks for the first time:

“Martha is inside.”

He leads the horse away towards the stable.

pages.heading: The Hall
pages.text:
The door stands open.

You pick up your luggage and go in. The hall is darker than outside and your eyes take a few seconds. Stone floor, a wooden staircase going up, and on the right a door half open, with the sound of pots coming through it and a woman’s voice. She is giving somebody instructions, quickly.

The voice stops.

“You’re here?”

She comes out from behind the door. Forties, flour on her apron, and she wipes her hands on it twice before putting one out. “Martha. The kitchen is mine.”

She looks you over, and does not disguise doing it.

“Road all right, was it? Gregor does not talk much. Do not take it to heart, he is like that with everybody.” She has already turned to go further in as she says it, so that you can only follow. “Supper at six. Go up and look at your room first. Elena.”

There are footsteps on the stairs.

pages.heading: The Room
pages.text:
Elena walks half a step ahead of you with her hands folded in front of her. She does not say a word, and only turns side-on at the corners to indicate the way.

The room at the end of the upstairs corridor. She pushes the door open and stands in the doorway. She does not come in.

The room is not large. A bed, with fresh sheets, the corners folded down square. A wardrobe, a desk. The desk faces the window, and the window faces the direction of Maplegate Avenue, which has gone dark by now.

The desktop is dark wood. There is a rectangular mark on it, paler than the wood around it. The four edges are very straight. Something stood there once, and stood there long enough for the wood around it to darken past it.

“Everything has been put in order,” Elena says. It is the first thing she has said. “If you need anything else, tell me.”

She steps back and pulls the door to.

Her footsteps go a few paces along the corridor, stop for a moment, and only then go on down.

pages.heading: The First Night
pages.text:
Once it has gone fully dark outside, the estate is quieter than you expected.

There is none of the floor of noise a city has. What you can hear comes separately: one movement in the stable off in the distance, the wind going through the maples, water dripping somewhere. Every sound can be heard on its own, with whole silence in between them.

You open your case halfway, and close it again.

From tomorrow, this estate is yours to run for thirty days.
